There is no doubt that, as for the miracles, what is intended by them is the establishing of prophethood and of the proof against people; in this, certainty is required, because upon it rests the foundation of faith. For that reason they cannot be treated in the way the other material of the biography is treated. But for all that, they say that by the totality of these, certainty is attained; so whatever is additional to that is in the position of what is taken as corroboration.

As for the refutation of the objections raised against the biography of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: in former times the most important book composed on this is the book al-Shifāʾ by the judge ʿIyad, as we have mentioned before, and also its commentaries, the commentaries on this book. Afterwards there came the objections that combine the Sunnah and the biography; and among the most important books in refuting those who raise them is the book al-Sunnah wa-Makānatuhā fī al-Tashrīʿ al-Islāmī by Professor Mustafa al-Sibaʿi, and likewise the book of al-Muʿallimi in his refutation of Abu Rayyah, and the book Difāʿ ʿan Abī Hurayrah likewise — the books that refute objections, the defence of the Sunnah and the creed and so on. There are very many books refuting the objections of the orientalists and their hangers-on. And among the books that refute the objections concerning Islamic history generally, and especially the caliphs and the Companions and what arose between them, is the book al-ʿAwāṣim min al-Qawāṣim by Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi. This book was printed long ago in full under the supervision of Shaykh ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Badis; then Muhibb al-Din al-Khatib selected a portion from it which he extracted and printed, and this is today famous under the name of the book — but the fact is that it is only a portion of the book, a small portion. Muhibb al-Din al-Khatib's book has now been printed in eighteen editions, and it is only an offshoot of it …

As for the praise with which the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was praised: some specialised books have likewise been composed on it, such as the book al-Minaḥ fī al-Madḥ by Ibn Sayyid al-Nas, in which he mentioned only the Companions' praise of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace — what the Companions praised the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, with. And after that many prophetic panegyrics were composed, some of them complete collections of poetry, such as the dīwān of al-Burʿi: many of the odes in it are in praise of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. Al-Burʿi the Imam — many of his odes are in praise of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

Likewise the odes of al-Busiri became famous, and that because of his excellence in poetry and his mastery of it, so that there was none in his age like him. That is why he said of himself:

*I am the Hassan of your praise, and when* … in his Hamziyyah: "I am the Hassan of your praise" — he compared himself with Hassan ibn Thabit in praise. "And when I lament for you, then I am al-Khansaʾ" — he compared himself in elegy with al-Khansaʾ. His odes were also commented upon, and that increased their fame among people: the Burdah was commented upon and the Hamziyyah was commented upon; Dallis commented on the Hamziyyah with a lengthy commentary.

As for these extravagances that may occur, he has a justification in them, namely that the pronouns which some people, upon reading them — and especially one who is not among the people of rhetoric — may suppose to refer back to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, he did not intend to refer back to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, but intended to refer them back to God Most High. The interweaving of pronouns in this way is acceptable in the language, as in the words of God Most High: {Indeed We have sent you as a witness and a bearer of good tidings and a warner, that you may believe in God and His Messenger and honour him and revere him and glorify Him morning and evening} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:8–9). For the pronoun in His words "and glorify Him morning and evening" is not for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to whom the preceding pronouns refer, but is for God, mighty and majestic.

And that is likewise what he intended in some places of his Burdah; but some people understand that in a mistaken way, as though he meant by it the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

Yes, by this is meant God, mighty and majestic:

*For among your bounty are this world and its rival* … — this is praise of God, mighty and majestic. But this occurs often in rhetoric and is frequent in poetry, and in the Qur'an too there are many parallels to it. Yes, he was without doubt a Sufi, but not like Ibn al-Farid, for example. And he is also highly creative in poetry and in description and in praise. So for all that, it may be that because of his love for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, there were some marks of divine honour that appeared at his hands, and some states that come upon some of those who love, from reciting his odes.

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God bless and grant peace to our Prophet … As for the science of Islamic history: it is one of the Islamic sciences which were originally subordinate to the science of hadith and the science of exegesis, and then became independent in composition and stood alone. Its definition is that it is the knowledge of the events of the years, the deaths of eminent men, and the reports of kings. So it is concerned with these three matters essentially: the events of the years and what occurs in them of important matters, such as the conquest of lands and the important signs in creation, and likewise the campaigns — even the days of the enemy in the lands of the Muslims; and likewise what relates to the deaths of eminent men, so as to set out the eminent men of every age and the dates of those eminent men; and then after that the reports of kings, their accession and their deposition and what relates to that.

And by its definition its subject matter is known: its subject matter is the stories of those who have passed. To that may be added the lessons for the future, for time repeats itself. That is why many of the historians place this consideration in their books and point by it to the future. Al-Dhahabi in his history named it the Book of Lessons in the Reports of Those Who Have Passed (al-ʿIbar bi-Akhbār man Ghabar) — and "the lessons" is for our taking a lesson from the reports of the predecessors. Likewise Ibn Khaldun named his book: the Book of Lessons and the Register of the Subject and the Predicate in the Reports of Those Who Have Passed, and the Reports of the Arabs and the Persians and the Berbers and Those of the Greatest Authority Who Were Their Contemporaries.

So he made it a register of the subject and the predicate: the subject for the reports of those who have passed and the predicate for the future. In this there is an allusion to the structure of the nominal sentence with its subject and its predicate; and likewise that he first makes the persons known and then mentions the judgement upon them by their qualities, because the subject is definite and the predicate is the judgement upon it. The predicate is a judgement upon the subject, and a judgement cannot be made upon the unknown.

And likewise he alludes also to the report (khabar), which is the story, together with the subject (mubtadaʾ), which is the origin — that is, the origin of the stories and their causes. The subject is the origin of the story and the predicate is the story itself which is related, because the khabar is what admits of being true or false.

And like that is what Ibn Kathir did in his history, for he named it al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah, "The Beginning and the End": the beginning for the reports of those who have passed and the end for what will come in the future ….

As for the founder of this science, he is not known, and especially since it is among the sciences of the ancients; for every nation used to give attention to its history and concern itself with recording it. The kings of the Persians of old gave attention to recording their histories, and likewise the kings of China. God, glorified and exalted, argued in His Book against the Jews by history, which also suggests that the Jews used to give attention to history. He said, exalted is He: {Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but was upright, submitting; and he was not of the idolaters} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:67), until He said: {and the Torah and the Gospel were not sent down until after him} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:65). This is an argument from history: the Jews claimed that Abraham was a Jew, and He said: "and the Torah was not sent down until after him" — how could he be a Jew when Judaism has its origin in the sending down of the Torah? And the Christians claimed that he was a Christian: how could he be so when the Gospel was not sent down until after him, and the arising of Christianity is from the sending down of the Gospel?

Likewise, in the refutation of some of their reports, the argument from history also came in the Qur'an, in the words of God Most High: {All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel forbade to himself before the Torah was sent down. Say: then bring the Torah and recite it} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:93). This is an argument against the Jews from history: "before the Torah was sent down".

Among the Muslims, one of the first who gave attention to history and set it down was ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, may God be pleased with them both; but he wrote nothing on it, and only used to gather the stories and relate them. It is said that ʿAqil ibn Abi Talib gave attention to this discipline before him, and he was the genealogist of the Arabs and knowledgeable about their days and their histories, and used to relate them in the mosque of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in the days of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. And before that, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, was concerned with the genealogies of the Arabs and their reports. That is why, when Hassan came to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, asking permission to lampoon Quraysh, he gave him permission and said: How will you lampoon them when I am one of them? He said: I shall draw you out from among them as a hair is drawn out of dough. He said: Go to Abu Bakr and seek his help. Then he said: Lampoon them, and the Holy Spirit is with you. And when his poetry reached Quraysh, in it was:

*And the noble of stock among the family of Hashim* … So Quraysh said: This is poetry, by God, from which Ibn Abi Quhafah was not absent. For the children of ʿAbd al-Muttalib were twelve; and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and Abu Talib and some of their brothers — their mother was Fatimah bint ʿAmr ibn ʿAʾidh ibn ʿImran ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar ibn Makhzum. That is why he said: *And the noble of stock among the family of Hashim are the sons of the daughter of Makhzum, while your father is the slave.* Here he is lampooning Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, the direct cousin of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

Among the first who composed in this science is Khalifah ibn Khayyat, who is nicknamed Shabab and who is a teacher of al-Bukhari. He composed his book al-Tārīkh and gave attention in it to three matters among the events of the years: the first, who of the eminent men died in that year; the second, who led the winter expedition in it and who led the summer expedition; and the third, who led the hajj for the people. He gave attention to these matters only. The shātiyah is the raiding detachment that goes out in winter, and the ṣāʾifah is the party that goes out for striving in God's path in summer. His book is not a large one.

He also composed the book al-Ṭabaqāt, devoted to the classes of the transmitters. Then after him came Muhammad ibn Saʿd, the scribe of al-Waqidi, who gave attention to some history in his book al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā, and especially to what relates to the transmitters' places of residence and the cities in which they settled. He gave this outstanding attention, so that he is the greatest reference in what concerns residence in the various regions: he gives the classes of the inhabitants of Medina, and of the inhabitants of Basra, and of the inhabitants of Kufa, and of the inhabitants of Egypt, and of the inhabitants of Syria, and distinguishes them by that. Likewise he gave attention to separating the men from the women, and he is the first who separated the women and gave them an independent book at the end of his book.

Then came the Imam al-Bukhari, who gave attention to the history of the people of hadith in particular and composed on it his book al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr; and it has been mentioned before among the books of the men. But given that he also gave attention to some of the transmitters' deaths — though he did not give them complete attention, for of many transmitters he mentioned nothing relating to their dates — still, in view of the name of the book, since its name is "the History", it was counted among the books of history. When al-Bukhari presented this book to Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, he looked into it and marvelled and said: It is nothing but magic. For it is the first book arranged by the letters of the alphabet, by the first letters of the names of the transmitters and then the following and the following; so Ishaq counted it as magic, because God opened for al-Bukhari in it a remarkable opening in arrangement, and from it all the lexicons set out.

Among the famous of those who composed in this science is Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Abu Jaʿfar, who died in the year three hundred and ten. It has been mentioned before that he is also among the first authors in exegesis. He began his history with some of the stories of the prophets and the ancients and the reports of the kings and the earlier nations, and that is why he named his book Akhbār al-Umam wa-l-Mulūk. But as for what relates in it to the reports of the Companions, most of it is transmitted by a route that is not established: either by the route of Abu al-Saʾib from Abu Salih — and this is the route of the liars, as is known among the people of hadith, Muhammad ibn al-Saʾib al-Kalbi from Abu Salih; or by the route of al-Waqidi, and it has been mentioned before that he is abandoned; or by the route of Abu Mikhnaf, who was a partisan Shiʿi; or by the route of Ibn Abi Maryam, who is a liar also. And for all that, in it are many other stories and reports, some of them from his own observations and some of them from the mass-transmitted accounts that people related; and he recorded them in his book, so that it became a reference in this field.

Among those who likewise gave attention to recording these stories and reports is Ibn al-Athir the elder. In this family three scholars became famous: Ibn al-Athir the elder is the historian, the middle one is the grammarian, and the youngest is the hadith scholar and lexicographer, Abu al-Saʿadat, who composed Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl and composed al-Nihāyah fī Gharīb al-Ḥadīth. As for the elder, he is the one who composed his history which he named al-Kāmil. It is a well-stocked book which relied heavily on Ibn Jarir, but he added to it and gave the reports of the kings of his own time and the civil strife that took place in the days of the Abbasid state, and documented it because he was at the heart of events and was close to the authorities in that age. He was one of the inhabitants of the city of Mosul, a city lying between Diyar Bakr and the lands of central Iraq and between the two rivers and the lands of the Turks; and it is likewise the road of the whole East to Syria, the outlet of the whole East upon Syria. At the beginning of the Abbasid state it was a small province; and when Harun al-Rashid appointed Yazid ibn Mazyad over it, he entered it having had a standard tied for him on a lance, and when he entered from the fortress the lance on which the standard was broke, and he took that as an evil omen. So ʿAli ibn al-Jahm, one of the famous poets who was accompanying him, said:

*The breaking of the standard was no cause for misgiving, but* … he saw the smallness of the province — that is, Yazid thought Mosul too little to be his province. So Harun al-Rashid enlarged it at that time and made it one of the frontier capitals; and the situation continued so until it later became an independent state, the capital of an independent state subordinate to the Islamic caliphate in Baghdad.

In general his book is also well arranged: events are not repeated in it and cross-references are made to various places — unlike the case of Ibn Kathir's book. And Ibn Kathir's book, al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah, is likewise a well-stocked register of reports, and he gathered in it the history of the East and the West; but its arrangement is not good, because the reports are interwoven in it with the biographies of men. He proceeds in arrangement by the years, and then when the death of one of the famous men falls in one of the years, he goes off into narrating the life of that man and so mentions years past and years to come, and the chronology becomes interwoven. Also, Ibn Kathir, may God have mercy on him, although he is one of the leading authorities in hadith and exegesis, did not give much attention to verifying the anecdotes and stories in the book.

And among the remarkable things is that most of the historians, even in the stories they lived through and the matters they ought to have related, end their books before reaching them. For it is important for the historian to write first what is in his own age, of what he witnessed, because that is what is sound in his own view; and in general the historians do not occupy themselves with this. They write on the reports of the predecessors and rely on there being room and remainder in their lifetime, and he dies before recording his own history for us — except al-Dhahabi, may God have mercy on him, for he gave great attention to writing and was granted success in writing what was in the days of his own life in a number of his books, whether among them what was in the biographies of men, such as Tadhkirat al-Ḥuffāẓ and Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, or what was among them in pure history, such as Tārīkh al-Islām, for he continued it into the middle of his own life. And he composed some continuations upon some of the books of the predecessors in which he mentioned what he himself witnessed, such as his continuation of the Tārīkh Baghdād of al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, and other continuations he composed upon the books of the predecessors.

In general al-Dhahabi is the best of the historians in point of declaring stories and reports sound or weak and of verifying them; for in many cases he relates them with the chains, and impugns what is impugned among them, and relates his own observations and the strange things he saw.

As for the books named the histories of the lands, they come under the science of the men and the science of hadith, as has preceded — such as Tārīkh Baghdād, and Tārīkh Dimashq by al-Hafiz Ibn ʿAsakir, and Tārīkh Jurjān, and Tārīkh Iṣfahān, and the other books named "history", such as the three histories of Yahya ibn Maʿin. These are for the biographies of men, and in particular the men of hadith.

Then came Ibn Khaldun, who had an independent theory, namely the analysis of events so as to extract

the influence of the science of society — the influence of association upon people. So he understands situations not individually but collectively, and analyses the causes that lead to events. Ibn Khaldun's history is distinguished by the Introduction, which is … And in the days when he was in the Maghrib he was gathering all the histories of the Maghrib; and when he went to the East in a ship, the ship sank and he was saved from it, and his books were drowned. Many upheavals took place in his lifetime and he witnessed many remarkable events. He survived the plague that destroyed people in Tunis, and none of his household was saved but he; and his lineage was lost to him, so that he did not know how many generations lay between him and his furthest ancestor, who is Khaldun. He knows that he is his ancestor, but does not know how many fathers lie between him and him — whether between him and him there are three fathers or four or three or two, he does not know. The genealogist of the world, and he does not know what lies between himself and Khaldun of fathers, because of this plague that did away with everything. So his history was one that gave great attention to the reports of states and policies and wars.

The Maghribis and the Andalusians likewise gave particular attention to their own histories. Ibn Hazm was among the famous historians in Andalusia, and he met with much harm on account of that, for he was subjected to many trials because of his writing in history — his writing about the genealogies of certain people. And so too the Imam Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, who is Ibn Hazm's teacher, gave attention to history and wrote in particular on the Companions; he is the one who composed the book al-Istīʿāb fī Tarājim al-Aṣḥāb, that is, the Companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. This is one of the important fields of history, because when a transmitter's companionship is established, his uprightness is not investigated, since all the Companions are upright; but how his companionship is established — that is what requires verification and deliberateness. Al-Hafiz Abu Nuʿaym al-Isfahani composed on the knowledge of the Companions; and Ibn al-Athir likewise composed Usd al-Ghābah fī Maʿrifat al-Ṣaḥābah; and he himself composed this book of his, al-Istīʿāb bi-Tarājim al-Aṣḥāb; and al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar composed his book al-Iṣābah fī Tamyīz al-Ṣaḥābah. Ibn Hazm also composed on the Companions from whom the giving of legal opinions is transmitted; and Ibn Hazm gathered the summary of his learning in genealogy in his book al-Jamharah fī al-Ansāb. We shall single out the books of genealogy in particular for some detail, because they are distinct from the science of Islamic history.

Among those who gave attention to history in Andalusia is Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib, the holder of the two vizierates, the famous man of letters and poet. His compositions are very many, and he composed the book al-Iḥāṭah fī Tārīkh Gharnāṭah and other books on the history of Andalusia.

Likewise among the famous historians in Andalusia is Ibn Bassam, who composed the book al-Dhakhīrah fī Maḥāsin Ahl al-Jazīrah; and then finally al-Maqqari, who composed Nafḥ al-Ṭīb min Ghuṣn al-Andalus al-Raṭīb. It is in origin a biography of Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib, but he went beyond that and wrote about the whole of Andalusia and described its regions and fixed their locations, and mentioned the eminent men who entered it, and mentioned the poems and reports and stories that have come concerning it, and the biographies of its people, and the revolts; and it was an important historical book. Likewise in the Maghrib a number of authors in history became famous, and among the famous of the later ones among them is al-Marrakushi, who composed *al-M-gh-r-b* on the reports of the Maghrib, and al-Nasiri al-Salawi, who composed al-Istiqṣāʾ li-Akhbār al-Maghrib al-Aqṣā.

Likewise the people of Egypt gave attention to its history from various aspects. Among the first who gave attention to the history of Egypt is al-Kindi, who composed Akhbār al-Quḍāt and then composed Akhbār al-Wulāt, giving attention only to those who held the judgeship in Egypt from the time of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs. Likewise al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar composed a number of books relating to the history of Egypt, such as Rafʿ al-Iṣr ʿan Akhbār Quḍāt Miṣr, and such as his other book al-Durar al-Kāminah fī Aʿyān al-Miʾah al-Thāminah, and such as his other book on the people of his own age whom he met and who gave him licences to transmit.

His student al-Sakhawi composed a large, well-stocked book on the reports of the people of Egypt; and al-Suyuti likewise composed Ḥusn al-Muḥāḍarah bi-Akhbār Miṣr wa-l-Qāhirah; and al-Yafiʿi composed the book Mirʾāt al-Zamān; and Ibn Taghri Bardi likewise — and his name is pronounced with the shortened yāʾ and with the defective yāʾ, Taghri Bardi or Taghrā Bardā — composed his book al-Nujūm al-Zāhirah fī Akhbār Miṣr wa-l-Qāhirah.

Among the historians who give attention to the histories of the regions generally, Ibn Khallikan became famous, who composed his book Wafayāt al-Aʿyān; and this book was the occasion for many other compositions, of additions to it and supplements and corrections and so on, for many continuations were composed upon it, such as Fawāt al-Wafayāt by al-Safadi … yes, a number of those who composed additions upon it — yes, al-Wāfī bi-l-Wafayāt.

Likewise al-Samʿani, may God have mercy on him, took another direction in history and gave attention only to the affiliations of eminent men: he gave attention to them from the linguistic side first, and then after that gives their biographies. So every affiliation that became well known in history — whether to a country or to a tribe or to a craft or a trade or the like — he explains that affiliation and then sets out those who became famous by this affiliation, with their names and their dates and their biographies. His book al-Ansāb is among the important books in this field, especially as he explains the strange affiliations to cities, or an obsolete affiliation to unknown villages.

As for what relates to genealogies, it is among the complements of history — it is in fact a science among the complements of history, because genealogies follow upon merits; otherwise all people belong to Adam, and Adam is from dust. But people are disposed by nature to boast of their genealogies and to give attention to them. It has come in the sound hadith from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: Two matters of the age of ignorance are in my community, and they are in them — the shirk of taking omens, and boasting of genealogies.

The Children of Israel used to give attention to genealogies in ancient times; and among the Arabs likewise there became famous those who gave attention to their genealogies. They used to boast of them and to make it one of the rites of the hajj, so that among the rites of the hajj with them was that a contest of boasting in genealogies and forefathers would be held. That is why God Most High said: {as you remember your fathers, or with a stronger remembrance} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:200). And markets used to be held for that, and the assemblies were set up in them for this purpose — among them the market of ʿUkaz at Taʾif, and the market of Dhu al-Majaz, which was near Taʾif also, and the other markets that used to be held for this purpose, and the market of Banu Qaynuqaʿ at Medina.

These genealogies, though much disagreement has arisen in them — for among the tribes of the Arabs there were some that wavered, so that it is not known whether they are of the ʿAdnani or of the Qahtani line, and they are numerous tribes, and especially since they are many in number, such as all the tribes of Qudaʿah, which are very many; the Arabs used to make them a byword for number. Among the tribes of Qudaʿah are Banu Kalb ibn Wabarah ibn Ilhaf ibn Qudaʿah, and likewise Banu ʿUdhrah, and others of the tribes of Qudaʿah; and they settled among ʿAdnan, while it appears that their origins are from Qahtan. And likewise among the wavering tribes are Banu Khuzaʿah: it is said Khuzaʿah ibn Malik ibn Himyar, and it is said rather that they are of the ʿAdnani line. And so many of the tribes waver in their genealogies.

Even within a single tribe many clans have become well known whose affiliation to the root of the tribe is doubted. Banu Tamim have many tribes, but the affiliation of many of them to Tamim ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tabikhah is doubted. That is why al-Farazdaq says:

*The genealogists, when they count to Tamim, count al-Rabab and the family of Saʿd, and al-Marʾī falls out of the middle of them as idle talk.*

It has come from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: The genealogists have lied about what is beyond ʿAdnan. And the meaning of "the genealogists have lied" is either by distortion, or by the biographies, or by mentioning something of their reports, or even by addition and omission — all of that is possible. And it has come from him, may God bless him and grant him peace, in sound hadiths, that he traced his lineage up to ʿAdnan; and likewise he mentioned that he is of the progeny of Ishmael son of Abraham, and that is established from him in a number of hadiths.

Likewise in his maternal relationships he often affirms them; but when Banu Kindah came to him and said, Messenger of God, we are the sons of Akil al-Murar and you are his son, he said: We, the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, do not trace our lineage to anyone else. Akil al-Murar is one of the famous kings of Banu Kindah and is the ancestor of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, on the maternal side; but he did not wish to affiliate to him.

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, comes the tracing of the lineage up to Adam, and that has come from a number of genealogists; and this can be maintained consistently and is known in the genealogies of the tribes of the Arabs. But it is difficult to attend to in the genealogies of the non-Arabs — except that some of the kings of the non-Arabs sought the help of certain genealogists, who connected their genealogies for them; and when the Ottoman state grew strong they found genealogists who traced their lineage up to Adam, peace be upon him. So the root of genealogy that can be studied and investigated is essentially the genealogies of the Arabs, or the genealogies of the Children of Israel also, because some of these have roots — as the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to Safiyyah bint Huyayy in establishing her lineage to Aaron son of ʿImran, the brother of Moses, peace be upon them both.

Many books have been composed on genealogy. Among them are those relating to the genealogies of certain tribes, and the most important of these is the genealogies of Quraysh. Musʿab ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Thabit ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam composed on it the book Nasab Quraysh; and likewise his nephew al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar — and Bakkar's name is Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Musʿabi — composed a book which he named Jamharat Ansāb Quraysh. As for Nasab Quraysh by al-Zubayri, it was printed long ago at the hands of one of the orientalists, and is printed in the Dhakhāʾir al-ʿArab series in full, though there are some errors in it, for it is printed from a single manuscript copy. As for the book of al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar, it has not been printed; the historian Mahmud Shakir printed an extract from it last year or the year before — only an extract from a book from the last part of the genealogies of the Banu al-Zubayri, and in it is mention of some of the genealogies of Banu Asad.

People likewise gave attention to the genealogies of the prophetic line, because of the rulings of the Sharia that follow from these genealogies. Qurashi descent is a condition in the imamate, so that in establishing it there is need to establish lineage. That is why the Abbasid caliph who arose in Egypt after the fall of the caliphate in Baghdad was not given allegiance until he had established his lineage before the judges and they had given judgement upon it. He was black, and the Abbasids are known for whiteness, but his mother was a black slave; so he established his lineage before the judges and the people gave him allegiance in Egypt, and he was the father of the Abbasid caliphs in Egypt. Likewise the prophetic line: Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib and their clients are forbidden to receive charity, and certain juristic rulings relate to that, and for this reason people gave attention to recording their genealogies — and especially the Talibids, for a number of books have been composed on their genealogies, and even on their deaths and the places where they fell, a number of books have been composed. And likewise the genealogies of the Companions generally, and the genealogies of the Mothers of the Believers, and the genealogies of the famous leading scholars: on all of that a number of books have been composed. Among the comprehensive books on genealogy is the book of Abu Muhammad ʿAli ibn Hazm which he named al-Jamharah, and likewise the book of al-Qalqashandi, and the book of al-Suwaydi, Nihāyat al-Arab fī Dhikr Qabāʾil al-ʿArab.

Ahmad al-Badawi al-Umawi al-Majlisi al-Shinqiti composed his versification which he named ʿAmūd al-Nasab. It is a long versification that gathered the genealogies of the Arabs and gave attention essentially to the genealogies of those between whom and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, there is a relation of kinship. So he began first with the lineage of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, up to ʿAdnan; then he began with the progeny of ʿAdnan in detail — the tribes that are of the progeny of ʿAdnan other than the main line of descent; then he came down to Maʿadd and gave the tribes of the progeny of Maʿadd other than the main line, and he defers the main line until he mentions it last of all. The last he mentioned is Banu Hashim; they are the last of the ʿAdnanis he included. Then he went to the Qahtanis, and began them with the Ansar — he versified the genealogies of the Ansar — and then began with the people nearest and then next nearest to the Ansar, among the Qahtanis.

This is the most important of what relates to genealogies; and we return to the other preliminaries in the science of Islamic history.

We have mentioned its definition and the investigation of its founder and likewise of its subject matter. As for its relation to the other sciences, it is a relation of partial overlap, because it shares with the science of the men in many of its investigations, and likewise with the other sciences. The science of juristic riddles is mostly studied by the people of history, because it belongs to the biographies of men; and likewise many juristic questions are studied in the science of biography generally, among them the biographies of the scholars of the juristic schools — the books that have given attention to the biographies of the scholars of the juristic schools, some of which we mentioned before, I believe, in the science of the men ….

As for the relation of this science, as we mentioned, to the other sciences: we mentioned that many of the questions — the juristic questions, and the juristic riddles and their solutions — are mentioned in the biographies of the scholars. Among these are the books composed on the biographies of the scholars of the schools. In the Hanafi school, for example, the book al-Ṭabaqāt al-Saniyyah fī Tarājim al-Ḥanafiyyah, and the book al-Jawāhir al-Muḍiyyah, and the book Tāj al-Tarājim, and other books of Hanafi biography. In the Maliki school, the book al-Dībāj by Ibn Farhun and its continuations, among them Tawshīḥ al-Dībāj by al-Qarafi, and among them likewise Nayl al-Ibtihāj bi-Taṭrīz al-Dībāj by Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti; and the books of biography specific to particular lands, such as Fatḥ al-Shakūr min Tarājim ʿUlamāʾ al-Takrūr — yes, and the book al-Madārik by the judge ʿIyad, which is called al-Madārik and is called Tartīb al-Madārik; and such as Shajarat al-Nūr al-Zakiyyah fī Tarājim al-Sādah al-Mālikiyyah, by Muhammad al-Husayn Makhluf, or Muhammad Husayn Makhluf. And likewise in the Shafiʿi school, the book Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyyah al-Kubrā by Ibn al-Subki, ʿAbd al-Wahhab ibn ʿAli ibn ʿAbd al-Kafi; and the book Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyyah by Ibn Qadi Shuhbah; and the book Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyyah also by al-Isnawi — there are a number of authors who composed on the classes of the Shafiʿis, and likewise on the biographies of the leading scholars themselves. Likewise on the classes of the Hanbalis there is a book by Ibn Rajab, and the book of Ibn Muhlah, and the book of Ibn al-Jawzi.

And the grandson of al-Jawzi, his daughter's son, likewise composed even on general history and unrestricted biography, and composed his book al-Muntaẓam, which is among the extensive books of history. And likewise among the important and beneficial books of biography for tracing reports, in which he gives some scholarly weighings, is the book Shadharāt al-Dhahab by Ibn al-ʿImad al-Hanbali.

As for the source from which this science is drawn, it is from the stories that come by word of mouth and by transmission, and from poetry and transmitted reports. As for its merit, it is according to its usefulness; and there is no doubt that if you look over those who became famous in this science you will find them eminent figures among the eminent of the community, which shows you its merit, for none occupied themselves with it but the famous eminent men. And likewise its usefulness: among its uses is the distinguishing of the sound from the weak, and of the noble from others.

That is why al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, may God have mercy on him, uncovered the forgery by the Jews of the document which they forged in the name of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he had lifted the poll-tax from them, and which they produced in the days of one of the Abbasid caliphs. When they presented it to the caliph, he did not know what to do, so he gathered the scholars and they examined it and were perplexed: it was a document written on hide in an old script like the scripts of the Companions, and it was written that it was in the hand of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and upon it was the seal of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and in it was the testimony of a number of the Companions — until the document was presented to al-Khatib, and he spat upon it and reported that it was a forgery. The caliph asked him: from where did you get that? He said: it is written in it that among its witnesses are Saʿd ibn Muʿadh and Muʿawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, and the two never came together in Islam; for Saʿd was wounded on the day of the Confederates and died after his judgement on Banu Qurayzah in the fifth year of the Hijrah, while Muʿawiyah did not become a Muslim until the year of the Conquest, in the eighth year of the Hijrah. So how could the two testify to a single document? And the one who disbelieved was struck dumb.

And likewise in what relates to authenticating men and impugning them. For this reason al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Naysaburi, Ahmad ibn al-Bayyiʿ, when he heard a man transmitting from Hisham ibn ʿAmmar, asked him when he had entered Egypt; and he told him the year in which he had entered it; and he said: This shaykh met Hisham and he transmitted to him eleven years after his death. So by this the importance of history is known.

Likewise it is among the consolations that take grief away from a person; for when he recalls the stories of those who have passed and what they met of harm and what took place in their days of civil strife, he praises God for his own condition and does not think little of God's blessing upon him, and in it is consolation for what befalls him. And likewise, in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding, for in them is a steadying of people upon the road of truth. It is related from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak that he said: The stories of the righteous are a host among the hosts of God, by which God makes firm the hearts of His servants. And the confirmation of that from the Qur'an is the words of God Most High: {And all that We relate to you of the reports of the messengers is that by which We make your heart firm; and in these there has come to you the truth and an admonition and a reminder for the believers} (Sūrat Hūd 11:120).

Likewise it is among the things that raise the morale of peoples when they recall their glories and what took place in their history in the past. That is why the civilisation of the Persians almost returned after their defeat, on account of the Shuʿubiyyah — even among the Muslims. Among these are the Barmakids, who were among the caliphs' men of the Abbasids and among those close to them, and among the Muslims whose religion is not doubted; but they became inclined towards their own kind, towards the civilisation of the Persians, and gave attention to reviving it, even by renewing some of the images that belonged to the Persians, such as the images of the city of Antioch which were on its wall, to which people used to come from afar; and likewise the images of the ancients which were in the cities of Chosroes and the Īwān. Al-Buhturi described the images that were on the wall of Antioch and said:

*I kept my soul from what would defile my soul, and held myself firm when fate shook me* …, until he says:

*And when I saw the image of Anṭ… while the fates are present* …

Likewise among the uses of history is the bearing of witness over people; for this community are God's witnesses over His creation, as has come from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: You are God's witnesses in His earth; whomever you praise with good, the Garden becomes due for him, and whomever you speak ill of, the Fire becomes due for him. And people are witnesses. That is why, when a person dies, his lifetime is renewed by what is preserved of him, as Ibn Durayd, may God have mercy on him, said:

*A man is nothing but a tale after him* … And history bears witness over people by what they have done.

Then after this its ruling. The ruling on learning this science is that it is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah), except in the case of those who specialise in hadith and the like of the sciences that require this, for then it becomes individually incumbent upon him; and likewise for whoever sets himself up to give legal opinions, because he must know those by whose statements and views he gives opinions, and know their biographies, so that he may be at ease with their statements and with the uprightness of their condition.

As for the comprehensive name of this science, it is the science of Islamic history; and it is also called the science of genealogies, and is called the science of biography.

As for its questions, they divide into the beginnings — which are the reports of the beginnings of the creation of the universe and the accounts of the prophets — and then after that the stories of the states that preceded Islam, who inhabited the earth longer than the Muslims have inhabited it; and then after this the reports of the Arabian Peninsula in particular, from the time of Abraham's building of the Sacred House, peace be upon him, and the nations and peoples who passed the Sacred House between them; and likewise the genealogies of the Arabs within the Peninsula and the wars that arose among them — whether the wars that arose among themselves, which are called the days of the Arabs, or the wars that arose between them and others, the most famous of which in the age of ignorance is the war of Yemen which arose between the Arabs and the Abyssinians. In this war the Arabs sought the help of the Persians, and Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan its commander had sought the help of the Persians and brought the sons of Chosroes who became known as the Abnāʾ; they settled in Yemen and its kingship was theirs afterwards. That is why people came in delegations to Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan to congratulate him, and among those who came to him were ʿAbd al-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. And concerning him Umayyah says:

*Drink in good health, the crown upon you, resting at ease* … *drink in good health, for their ostrich has taken flight* … *those are noble deeds, not two bowls* …

And the war of Dhu Qar, which was between Banu Bakr ibn Waʾil and the Persians; and concerning it there is related from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: Today Banu Shayban have been given victory over Chosroes, and by me they were given victory. For Banu Shayban were given victory over Chosroes, and they were given victory only by the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace; so God turned the Persians back from reaching the Arabian Peninsula after that, in preparation for the message of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The victory of Banu Bakr ibn Waʾil over Chosroes and his flight from them became famous, so that one of the poets says … And Banu Tamim used before that to boast that they had the bow of Hajib. The Arabs' lands had suffered drought and they needed to pasture in Iraq, and Hajib, the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, was the lord of Banu Tamim; so he entered upon Chosroes to ask his permission for the Arabs to pasture in his land, and Chosroes asked him to give him a pledge, and he brought out for him his bow, an old worn bow. So the Arabs entered Iraq on account of that bow, and Banu Tamim used to boast of it, as the poet said:

*She vaunts over us with the bow of her Hajib* — Hajib of the bow; so too Tamim vaunts with the bow of her Hajib.

So one of the poets said:

*And you, at Dhu Qar, your swords inclined* …

For that reason Banu Shayban had a great name in the age of ignorance and in Islam, on account of this. Concerning it Marwan ibn Abi Hafsah says, in his praise of Maʿn ibn Zaʾidah, who is one of them:

*The sons of Matar on the day of encounter, as though they were* … *they protect the neighbour until it is as though* … *noble ones who in Islam became lords, and it was not* … *they are the people: if they speak they are right, and if they are called* … *and the doers cannot do their deeds* … *three like unto mountains, he granted them* … *his two days were alike to us and became confused* — *was it the day of his overflowing generosity or the day of his valour?*

Maʿn ibn Zaʾidah had given him a hundred thousand, and he came in to the caliph al-Mansur — and al-Mansur was described as a miser — and he said to him: Maʿn, did you give Marwan ibn Abi Hafsah a hundred thousand for his saying:

*Maʿn ibn Zaʾidah, by whom there increased* …?

He said: No, but for his saying:

*I never ceased on the day of al-Hashimiyyah declaring openly* … *and I protected his flank and was his shield* …

So he is claiming a favour upon the caliph, that he defended him and was before him fighting on his behalf on the day of al-Hashimiyyah — which is the day on which Banu Hashim prevailed over Banu Umayyah in their war. So he reversed the matter.

Likewise what relates to the portents that appeared before the birth of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace; and although these are studied in the biography, they are studied in history also. Then what there was of the history of the Arabs in the lifetime of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and of his Rightly Guided Caliphs — and this side in particular is what the biography has specialised in. Then after that, the Islamic states, whether they were great states such as the Umayyad caliphate and the Abbasid caliphate, or states subordinate to them, such as the minor states subordinate to the Umayyads and the Abbasids in the various regions.

And likewise the conquest of the lands and the remarkable things that took place in them. These, then, are the questions of this science.

As for the manner of teaching this science: its teacher must first be impartial, so that he does not incline after his own desire. For many people lose the chastity of the tongue when they speak about others, and so make their sword a keen, cutting blade against the honour of Muslims who have died — and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, may God have mercy on him, said: Those are bloodstains from which God purified our swords, so let us not defile our tongues by mentioning them.

Likewise he must compare the transmissions and go back to the various references so that he may see the story as it truly is; and likewise concentrate on what is beneficial, namely the lessons and the instruction, and not be concerned with mere historical narration in which there is no benefit; and likewise keep away from the interpretations that minds reject, of which the historians have produced a great deal — many of them abound in exaggerations that are not to be believed.

And like this is deliberateness in what concerns impugnment, when he hears the words of some contemporaries about others; for that is not to be accepted with absolute submission, and especially if the one impugning is beneath the one impugned and of a lower rank than he in learning and God-consciousness. And whoever teaches this science ought likewise to be a student of the other religious sciences, such as legal theory and exegesis and hadith, for that is among the things that help him to profit from this science and to give it due attention. And he can compare the events he has witnessed and lived through with past events, so that the repetition of historical experiences may become clear to him. This is the most important thing in this science.

As for Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari and the other leading scholars who wrote the stories transmitted from these abandoned and weak narrators, the cause of that is that they do not find many trustworthy narrators who speak in this field. We mentioned before, in the biography, that the people of the Sunnah erred in this field: they set out from their creedal principle of not speaking about what arose between the Companions and of turning away from it, and that led them to turn away entirely from the historical stories.

As for what relates to the manner of writing history, there is no doubt that there are many influences upon it. Among them, first, that the Muslims did not write down learning at the beginning, lest that be mixed with the revelation; for the Children of Israel, when they wrote their histories, brought them into their scriptures, and that was among the causes of the prohibition of writing at the beginning: "Do not write from me anything other than the Qur'an, and whoever has written from me anything other than the Qur'an, let him erase it."

Likewise what relates to the temperaments of kings and commanders, for many of them cannot be content that some of the vile deeds they committed and the great events they fell into should be written down; and the poets used to set some of that down in secret, so that recourse is had to poetry for that. Poetry contains some matters that may be riddles pointing to what lies behind them, and what lies behind them may not be understood at all. For that reason ʿAnbasah, one of the famous grammarians of the earliest period — and he is among the students of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hadrami, who is among the students of Abu al-Aswad al-Duʾali — was lampooned by one of the poets, who said:

*There was in ʿAbdan and the elephant a deterrent* … So he came in to Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who asked him: What is the elephant with which people taunt you? He said: Who taunts me with the elephant? He said: Indeed; did the poet not say: *There was in ʿAbdan and the elephant a deterrent for ʿAnbasah, who sent the rhymes to me*? He said: That is not what the poet said; he said only:

*There was in ʿAbdan and baseness a deterrent*. So he said: A matter one flees from to baseness must be a great matter — he knew that the elephant had a story, but one that is unknown and not to be discovered; he chose baseness in place of it.

And likewise when the disagreement arose between Thaʿlab and al-Mubarrad, it is said that al-Mubarrad lampooned himself on the tongue of Thaʿlab in order to establish his lineage, and said:

*We asked every tribe about Thumalah* … *so I said: Muhammad ibn Yazid is one of them* … *and al-Mubarrad said to me: leave my people alone* …

Likewise, those who set themselves up to write history are not free of partisanship for one of the states or one of the schools, and that appears clearly in their books. Whoever reads al-Suyuti's books on history will find severe animus against the Umayyads, because he was among those close to the Abbasid ribāṭ; so he hated the Umayyads with an intense hatred and gathered everything that was said about them, even if it was weak in his own view.

It is related from the Imam Ahmad that he said: Three things have no root — and he mentioned among them consensus and history and exegesis. These three — or the apocalyptic portents, which are future history itself. His words "three things" mean three important matters; "have no root" means that their roots are not sound, so that little of them is sound. But that does not mean that they have no existence, for the Imam Ahmad wrote on exegesis.

There is no doubt that attention to kings in the earliest period was greater than attention to the biographies of the scholars, because of influence: history is intended for influence upon the scene and upon peoples, and the influence of kings is more telling. Even so, some scholars have received of biographies what kings have not received, because of the abundance of their influence, and especially those of them who are followed and who have schools.

As for the modern age, there is nothing new in the field of history as regards the past — although some contemporaries have begun to write modern Islamic history, such as the spread of Islam by way of the call to Islam, and some of the campaigns of striving of the later ages which are not mentioned in the old registers, and likewise the biographies of the later ones. And among them have come those who write continuations upon the books of the predecessors. Professor Mahmud Shakir has a school of his own in the new Islamic history; Muhammad Qutb wrote How We Write History; and likewise among those who are concerned with this side is Mahmud ibn al-Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Arnaʾut, who continued the book Shadharāt al-Dhahab by Ibn al-ʿImad after editing it.

In every country, historians of that country have become famous who gathered the reports of that country in particular. In Morocco ʿAbd al-Hadi al-Tajir became famous; and in Mauritania al-Mukhtar ibn Hamid, whom people call the second Ibn Khaldun, since he composed his great book Ḥayāt Mūrītāniyā — the scholar-poet; he was among the people of learning, but poetry overshadowed him. This Ḥayāt Mūrītāniyā is thirteen huge, very large volumes, and some of the volumes are more than ten thousand leaves. And likewise in every country there are some historians of that country: in Najd some historians became famous who wrote only about the history of Najd and about some of the tribes that were in it; and likewise in the Hijaz there are many books on the history of the Hijaz, and especially the history of the Two Noble Sanctuaries; and likewise in Yemen, a great number of authors in this field.

Professor Mahmud Shakir's school in what concerns Islamic history and its writing is a modern school, concerned only with the ordering of events and with linking history and geography as well, and with the discussion of environment and demographic research essentially, and the application of what relates to population theories and the like, linking them to the sequence of events.

As for research into the minor states that have creedal deviations, and especially the Shiʿi states and the Khawarij: no specialised books have been devoted to them, except that some historians have specialised in certain minor states, such as the ʿUbaydid state. It had a far-reaching effect and lasted a long period and arose in al-Mahdiyyah in Tunisia, then moved to Egypt and built Cairo; and the people of the Sunnah suffered great harm from it, for its rulers used to slaughter the scholars and assassinate them and perpetrate outrages against them. And like that are some of the Shiʿi states whose Shiʿism was moderate, in which there was not that Shiʿism that leads to harm against the people of the Sunnah — such as the state of Banu Hamdan. This state's princes had Shiʿism in them, but they were people of moderation and balance and people of striving in the path of God, and especially Sayf al-Dawlah. Sayf al-Dawlah was a cause of the repelling of the Crusaders from Syria and from the whole Islamic state; and likewise the repelling of the Russians, who had raids in his days — he is the one who repelled them; and he repelled the Tatars and delayed them for centuries. That is why Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi said of him:

*And how can the Byzantines and the Russians hope to destroy her* … And he truly terrified the Westerners for a time, until al-Mutanabbi said of him:

*……… until you left her, and there remained none but those whom the blades protected* … *the patricians weep for them in the darkness* … *for you are Abu al-Hayjaʾ ibn Hamdan, and Hamdan is Hamdun, and Hamdun is Harith* … *those are the eye-teeth of the whole caliphate* …

And he says of him also, in describing the king of the Byzantines who lost his son Constantine in one of the battles in the lands of Turkey — he immortalised it in his famous ode:

*For your eyes is what the heart meets and has met* … *and I was not one into whose heart love enters* … *and between contentment and displeasure and nearness and distance* … *and the sweetest love is that whose lord is in doubt of union* … *and one drunk with coquetry, sated with the fresh breeze* … *and one of sweet, gleaming front teeth, bright* … *and the necks of gazelles, like your neck, visited me* … *and not everyone who loves is chaste when he is alone* …, until he says in it:

*We bid them farewell while separation is among us as though it were* … *cutting, sharp — the weaving of David beside them* … *gentle towards the kings of the armies, as though they were* … *they are led to them* …, until he says:

*The king of the Byzantines saw your delight in bounty* … *and wrote from a land whose reaching is far* … *and there went from it every journey of his messenger* … *and when you wrote to him before this* …

The domestic is a commander among the commanders of the Byzantines; his qadhāl is the back of his head. And indeed Sayf al-Dawlah used to do this: when he wrote to their king he wrote to him upon their bones, the bones of those killed among them. They were Shiʿah from before; they are of some of the Arab tribes into which Shiʿism entered in the days of the strength of Shiʿism in Iraq, and they are of Banu Taghlib, into whom Shiʿism entered long ago.

For the most part, all the Islamic principalities or states have written histories, and especially the non-Arab dynasties. The Turks, for example — people gave great attention to writing their history, and especially in the lands they conquered. For example, these lands which they conquered used formerly to be called the lands of the Byzantines; the Turks were formerly in Turkestan and were not the people of these lands, and these lands which they conquered and which are today called Turkey are in origin the lands of the Byzantines. A number of books have been composed on them, such as the book Nafāʾis al-Manẓūm fī Tarājim Afāḍil al-Rūm, which is printed; and likewise a number of books devoted to the biographies of the Ottoman kings; and likewise the Seljuks and the other kings of the East generally, of the Persian dynasties and others, and likewise even of the peoples beyond the river. The histories that give attention to these and describe their regions and their cities are many.

And one kind of history book is concerned only with the description of lands, such as the book Muʿjam al-Buldān by Yaqut al-Hamawi. Yaqut composed many lexicons, among them for example Muʿjam al-Udabāʾ and Muʿjam al-Shuʿarāʾ and Muʿjam al-Buldān. In Muʿjam al-Buldān he describes all the Islamic regions that have any mention — even the places that are merely villages, or merely waters, or deserts; he describes them all geographically and mentions the stories that took place in them and the poems said about them.

As for the foundations of history: there have come in the hadith some foundations for history and geography. In geography, the words of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: The earth was folded up for me in the shape of a bird — Yemen its head, the Hijaz its breast, Egypt and Iraq its two wings, and Syria its tail. This hadith describes the Islamic territory: its extension was to the east and the west from the direction of the two wings, because the two wings extend and return; as for the head, nothing advanced to the south — even Abyssinia the conquest did not enter. And the tail likewise has a ruffling in it, and a scattering, as happened in eastern Europe and some of the lands beyond the river; but that broad expansion did not occur. That is why he said: Yemen is its head and the Hijaz its jawjaʾ — that is, its breast — and Egypt and Iraq its two wings, and Syria its tail.

As for history, in the hadith of Hudhayfah in the Musnad of the Imam Ahmad and elsewhere, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: There will be prophethood among you for as long as God wills it to be, then He will raise it up when He wills to raise it up. Then there will be a caliphate on the pattern of prophethood for as long as God wills it to be, then He will raise it up when He wills to raise it up. Then there will be a biting kingship for as long as God wills it to be, then He will raise it up when He wills to raise it up. Then there will be a coercive kingship for as long as God wills it to be, then He will raise it up when He wills to raise it up. Then there will be a caliphate on the pattern of prophethood — and then he fell silent.

This hadith contains the phases of this community's history and the setting out of its conditions. It began with prophethood, then with the Rightly Guided caliphate; then after that with the biting kingship, which was in the days of the Umayyads and the Abbasids and the Islamic states; and then after this began the coercive kingship, which is no longer a kingship belonging to the community but has become in the position of ownership — this is the meaning of coercion by way of compulsion; and this is what we are in. And after it will come a caliphate on the pattern of prophethood.

As for the meaning of history's repeating itself: God, glorified and exalted, placed in this world regular laws and made them lead to particular effects; then the world develops and moves away from those laws, and change takes place — "God does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves." Then when they take heed and return, matters go back to their courses, and the bow is taken up by the one who shapes it, and conditions become upright; then the cycle returns again, so that time turns in a new turning, and so on. And this must occur, and it is the established way of all life.

It does not mean that the repetition will be with the very same details as they were; what is meant by it is rather what relates to uprightness and moderation and what relates to deviation and disturbance. So they are cycles — cycles in history, in this way.

Likewise the expression of those people who say: creeds do not die. What is meant is that, in general, those creeds which were a trial will always have someone who holds to them; for it is a trial which God placed in the earth, so there must remain someone who calls to it and someone who is affected by it.

As for the travel-accounts of the scholars, these too are among the books that give a picture of lands and peoples and histories, and even of some of the customs and moral practices of which many historians are ignorant. The authors of travel-accounts also describe their observations and the matters they saw; but those who wrote their travel-accounts and are trustworthy are few. Some travel-accounts became famous for the great events that took place in them, such as the travels of Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi to the East, and such as the travels of al-Baji. Other travel-accounts became famous for geographical survey, such as the travels of Ibn Jubayr; and others spoke about peoples and their customs, such as the travels of Ibn Battutah, though in them are some rash claims; and others became famous only for attention to the people of learning and their lives, such as the travels of Ibn Rashid al-Qayrawani — and this travel-account became famous under the name Milʾ al-ʿAybah bi-mā Jumiʿa fī Ṭūl al-Ghaybah. And the same is what Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib wrote in his travel-account which he named Nufāḍat al-Jirāb fī-mā Jumiʿa fī Ṭūl al-Ightirāb. And such as the travel-accounts of some of our Shinqiti scholars, such as the travels of Shaykh Muhammad Yahya al-Walati, which is printed — Dar al-Gharb al-Islami printed it; and such as the travels of Shaykh Muhammad ibn al-Amin; and such as the travels of Ibn Tuwayr al-Jannah — there are a number of travel-accounts under this name. And the travels of al-Fudayl al-Waqilani likewise contained a precise description of many of the scenes he witnessed.

And likewise the travel-account of al-Ibrahimi — Bashir al-Ibrahimi, who is one of the founders of the Association of Scholars in Algeria — when he went to the East.

As for the work of the orientalists and their hangers-on in distorting history, it is very extensive, especially as they found the ground fit for this, since many of the Muslims are ignorant of their own history, and especially of the conquests on the peripheries. So these orientalists came and exploited the opportunity and interpreted the Islamic conquests and the striving in God's path with materialist interpretations, and sought out for them causes for which God has sent down no authority and which have no credibility in reality.

And likewise many of the series and films that have been produced treat historical questions, all of them lies and untrue tales; and even their interpretation of sound historical events was a false, counterfeit interpretation.

A question on genealogy, about the jurists' saying: people are trusted concerning their own lineages, or are believed concerning their lineages. To what extent is this rule to be taken into account in fiqh?

The answer is that this rule is sound from the juristic side, for lineage is acquired by prescription in the way that ownership is acquired by prescription; and there is disagreement over the period of prescription for property. It has been said ten years, and it has been said fifteen years, and it has been said thirty years. So the Hanafi school holds thirty years, the Shafiʿi and Hanbali schools fifteen years, and the Maliki school ten years — if within them a non-partner, that is a stranger, has held it and disposed of it while the owner is present and silent without excuse, then his claim is not accepted and neither is his evidence after that.

Likewise with lineages: if a person comes and claims that he is the son of so-and-so, and no one denies that, and nothing comes that contradicts it, and that is known for long periods and no one denies it, then lineage is established for him by that, so that he inherits from him, and so on. So what is meant is not that some person of doubtful lineage should come and attach himself to a particular lineage, claiming it while people do not believe him in it — that is not what is meant. What is meant is what people have kept silent about and accepted; this is what is acquired by prescription as all properties are. Whoever has held land from the outset is not asked: from where did you get this?

flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW (house rule 12). This is a well-known anecdote from the Arabic biographical literature, told here to illustrate that historical knowledge exposes forgery. In English it reads as a story about Jews collectively forging a document and being caught, ending with a scholar spitting on it and a Qur'anic tag ('and the one who disbelieved was struck dumb', Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:258). Nothing has been softened and nothing added; but the passage should not be published without a note on what kind of text it is. The same section also states that the Jews of old gave attention to genealogy and history, which is neutral, and the tape's argument from the Qur'an against Jewish and Christian claims about Abraham, which is exegesis rather than polemic.

The tape calls the Fatimids by the polemical name al-ʿUbaydiyyūn and says their rulers slaughtered and assassinated Sunni scholars, and describes al-Tabari's source Abu Mikhnaf as a partisan Shiʿi. translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

This is tape twelve of the Sheikh's course on the Islamic religious sciences (see IDs 448, 449, 450, 451, 453, 454 for other tapes). The first, shorter session completes an answer on the biography of the Prophet, the literature refuting objections to it, and the prophetic panegyrics. The second and much longer session is a complete treatment of the science of Islamic history — its definition, founder, subject matter, literature, uses, ruling and method of teaching — with a long excursus on genealogy.

The tape is largely bibliographical. Book titles are given in transliteration with diacritics and are not translated, except where the Sheikh himself unpacks the title's meaning — as with Ibn Khaldun's 'Register of the Subject and the Predicate', whose grammatical pun is the point of the passage and is therefore rendered in English with the technical terms alongside.

Hadith and narrator vocabulary follows the glossary: 'متروك' is 'abandoned', 'كذاب' is 'a liar', 'ثقات' is 'trustworthy narrators', 'المتواترات' is 'the mass-transmitted accounts'. Where the Sheikh impugns a named transmitter he is reporting the standard verdict of the hadith critics, and the English does not strengthen his wording.

The ruling given in this tape — that learning history is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah) which becomes individually incumbent on hadith specialists and on those who give legal opinions — is rendered with the glossary terms and is the only legal ruling in the record.
'الشعوبية' is rendered 'the Shuʿūbiyyah' in transliteration rather than by a gloss such as 'anti-Arab movement', since the Sheikh uses it as a proper name for a known historical current.

Proper names of non-Arab origin are given as the Sheikh gives them, including his own note on the two pronunciations of Ibn Taghri Bardi's name, which is preserved because it is an explicit remark about the name rather than an incidental spelling.
